analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 tax cuts permanent instead of letting them expire in 2010.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on June 27, 2001 and never received a vote or a committee hearing before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 tax law (EGTRRA) was written with a sunset: most of its tax cuts were scheduled to expire after 2010, which is what kept its official ten-year cost within budget limits. This bill would delete that expiration, making the rate cuts, estate tax repeal, and other provisions permanent. It also made one narrow change to the alternative minimum tax. The bill never moved past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthiest households gain the most: EGTRRA's top-rate cuts and its phased repeal of the estate tax concentrate their value at the top of the income scale, and making them permanent locks those gains in indefinitely. Higher-income earners generally gain from permanent rate cuts; owners of very large estates gain from permanent estate tax repeal. A narrow group of middle- and upper-middle-income taxpayers benefits from the bill's permanent fix to the alternative minimum tax exemption.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners and the largest estates

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Title IX of the 2001 tax law, the sunset provision that scheduled most of the tax cuts to expire after 2010, making them permanent. [S2] [S3]
Permanently sets the alternative minimum tax exemption for individuals at $49,000 (married, $35,750 single), rather than only for 2001-2004. [S3]
Sponsor Paul Ryan and 26 Republican cosponsors backed the bill. [S4]

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury and, ultimately, future taxpayers bear the cost: the sunset was the mechanism that kept the 2001 law's official ten-year cost inside its budget ceiling, so repealing it removes that ceiling and adds a permanent, growing gap between revenue and spending. Because the largest provisions (top-rate cuts, estate tax repeal) concentrate their value at the top, the permanent cost mostly finances tax reductions for the wealthiest households.

drawbacks.text: The sunset was the fiscal backstop of the 2001 law: the bill was written to expire so its official cost would fit budget limits. Repealing the sunset makes the cuts permanent and turns a temporary tax reduction into an open-ended, compounding claim on federal revenue. [S2] [S3]

The bill makes permanent the whole package, not just popular middle-class items: it locks in the estate tax repeal, which concentrates its benefit in the very largest estates, and the top-rate cuts. [S2] [S3]

The bill's alternative minimum tax fix is narrow: it raises the exemption to $49,000/$35,750 but does not index it or address the AMT's broader reach, leaving many taxpayers exposed to the tax the fix was meant to relieve. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's honest case is predictability: taxpayers and planners could rely on the tax cuts not expiring, and a small group gets a modest AMT break. But the design is tilted: the provisions whose value is most concentrated at the very top (estate tax repeal, top rates) are exactly the ones the sunset was designed to eventually end, and removing the sunset converts a decade-limited tax cut into a permanent structural revenue loss. There is no offsetting revenue in the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no markup, no hearing, and no floor vote until the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Paul Ryan introduced the bill on June 27, 2001 with 11 original cosponsors. [S1] [S3]
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which was its only committee action. [S5]
The bill gathered 26 Republican cosponsors but never received a vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003. [S4] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Treasury and future taxpayers are better off that this version died, because it would have permanently extended tax cuts whose value is concentrated at the top without paying for them. High earners and the largest estates, who would have gained most from permanence, gained nothing from this bill specifically — though Congress later extended many of the same cuts through other vehicles.

for.name: Paul Ryan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the sunset of the 2001 tax cuts.

against.name: Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or hearing; it died in his committee.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 sponsors (Ryan plus 26 cosponsors) were Republicans, and the bill never reached a floor vote where the parties' full positions could be recorded.

industries.industry: Wealthiest households and the largest estates
industries.note: Making EGTRRA permanent locks in the top-rate cuts and the estate tax repeal, whose benefits concentrate at the top of the income and wealth scale. The permanent revenue loss is borne by the Treasury and future taxpayers generally.

industries.industry: Taxpayers hit by the alternative minimum tax
industries.note: The bill permanently raises the AMT exemption to $49,000 (single $35,750), a modest, targeted benefit for middle- and upper-middle-income filers, though it leaves the exemption unindexed and the AMT's broader structure untouched.
